summary: Adam Behrens frames the talk around a philosophical question—what is a store?—tracing its evolution from clerk-fetched inventory, to self-service big box retail, to e-commerce, and now toward an agentic future. He defines a store as a location and protocol facilitating transactions between merchants, buyers, and a system. While e-commerce digitized merchandise and distribution, AI digitizes participants and their interactions, transforming static websites into merchant agents, consumers into consumer agents, and payment infrastructure into intent infrastructure. Two agentic futures are envisioned: agents browsing AI-optimized websites or agents accessing merchants programmatically via MCP servers and APIs. Core challenges include payments (virtual cards vs. delegated authentication via Visa), fuzzy intent (AI channel users show higher conversion and LTV), inventory availability (a unified API like Plaid for product data), and preference representation as a market design problem paralleling finance's solutions. Samsung exemplifies Fortune 500 adaptation with a three-step implementation: a unified API/MCP server across 10 verticals, connecting product data with brand/design systems, and building an AI subdomain for experimentation with generative interfaces and agentic transaction handling. Behrens argues stores evolve back toward conversation as their original form. In Q&A, he addresses adoption timeline (ChatGPT already bringing shopping experiences but full journey not yet in-app), payment mechanisms (stablecoins and crypto as conceptually native AI rails, credit cards as the practical bridge, agent-owned perpetual credit cards as a third option), super app dynamics (ChatGPT and Claude may aim for this, but model providers have different incentives than past tech companies, aligning with merchant goals), and revenue models (affiliate-style revenue or attribution-based data sharing rather than advertising).
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Evolution of the Store and the Agentic Future
sections.summary: Behrens traces the store's evolution from clerk-fetched inventory to big box retail to e-commerce, defining a store as a location and protocol facilitating transactions. He argues AI digitizes participants and interactions—merchant agents, consumer agents, and intent infrastructure—while the transaction goal remains unchanged. He poses the question of how a new generation of consumers, interfaces, and infrastructure will interact.

sections.title: Two Possible Agentic Futures
sections.summary: Behrens describes two futures: agents visiting AI-optimized websites that dynamically cut product catalogs and return rich content to chat interfaces, or agents using programmatic access via MCP servers and APIs that reason over calls and generate UI elements on the fly, with checkout hitting API endpoints instead of websites.

sections.title: Challenges: Payments, Intent, Availability, and Preferences
sections.summary: Three challenges are addressed. Payment: virtual cards vs. delegated authentication (Visa). Intent: AI channel users show higher conversion and LTV; currently forced via PDP URLs. Availability: product feeds and scraping are suboptimal; a unified API like Plaid for product data is proposed. Preferences are a market design problem—complex, changing, conflicting, with disincentive for honest reporting—paralleling finance's solution via third-party institutions.

sections.title: Intelligence Layer and Samsung Case Study
sections.summary: Behrens identifies the frontier as adding intelligence for real-time reasoning and coordination. Samsung's three-step implementation covers a unified API/MCP server across 10 verticals, connecting product data with brand/design systems for generative interfaces, and handling agentic transactions with payment flows for bot traffic—an inversion of typical website posture. He argues stores evolve back to their original form: conversation.

sections.title: Q&A: Adoption Timeline, Payment Rails, Super Apps, and Revenue Models
sections.summary: In Q&A, Behrens addresses adoption timeline (ChatGPT already incorporating shopping but full journey not yet in-app), payment mechanisms (stablecoins/crypto as conceptually native AI payment rails, credit cards as practical bridge, agent-owned perpetual credit cards as a third option), super app dynamics (ChatGPT and Claude may aim for this but model providers have different incentives than past tech companies, aligning with merchant goals around getting users to the right outcome), and revenue models (affiliate-style or attribution-based data sharing rather than advertising). He envisions a website inversion where instead of users going to the website, the website goes to a thousand different places.
